title: Definition
body_md:
A closed set $\mathcal{A} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is said to be \emph{uniformly globally asymptotically stable in probability} (UGAS$_p$) for $\mathcal{H}_s$ if it is both uniformly globally stable in probability and uniformly globally attractive in probability. Uniform global stability in probability requires that for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $\varrho > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that every random solution $x$ with $|x(0,0)|_{\mathcal{A}} \leq \delta$ satisfies $x(t,j) \in \mathcal{A} + \epsilon \mathbb{B}$ for all $(t,j)$ in its hybrid time domain, with probability at least $1 - \varrho$. Uniform global attractivity in probability requires that for every $\epsilon > 0$, $\varrho > 0$, and $R > 0$ there exists $s \geq 0$ such that every random solution $x$ with $|x(0,0)|_{\mathcal{A}} \leq R$ satisfies $x(t,j) \in \mathcal{A} + \epsilon \mathbb{B}$ for all $(t,j)$ in its domain with $t + j \geq s$, with probability at least $1 - \varrho$.
\hfill \qed
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{O} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be an open set. The set $\mathcal{O}$ is said to be \emph{uniformly globally recurrent} (UGR) for $(C,F,D,G,\mu)$ if for every $\varrho > 0$ and $R > 0$ there exists $s \geq 0$ such that every random solution $x$ with $|x(0,0)|\leq R$ satisfies the following with probability at least $1 - \varrho$: either the hybrid time domain of $x$ contains no $(t,j)$ with $t + j \geq s$, or there exists $(t,j)$ in the domain of $x$ with $t + j \leq s$ such that $x(t,j) \in \mathcal{O}$.
\hfill \qed
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The set $\mathcal{A}$ is uniformly globally asymptotically stable (UGAS) for system \eqref{eqn:hy_sys_def} if there exists $\beta \in \mathcal{KL}$ such that any solution $\xi$ satisfies $\lvert \xi(t,j) \rvert _{\mathcal{A}} \leq \beta(\lvert \xi(0,0) \rvert_\mathcal{A},t+j)$, for all $(t,j)\in\text{dom}(\xi)$. 
    \hfill \qed

label: defn:SGPAS
title: Definition
body_md:
\@gobble{defn:SGPAS} 
    The set $\mathcal{A}$ is semi-globally practically asymptotically stable (SGPAS) for an $\epsilon$-parameterized HDS $\mathcal{H}_{\epsilon}$ as $\epsilon \to 0$ if there exists $\beta \in \mathcal{KL}$ and for each $\mu,\nu >0$ there exists a $\epsilon^* >0$ such that, for each $\epsilon \in (0,\epsilon^*)$, any solution $\xi$ with $\lvert \xi(0,0) \rvert_{\mathcal{A}} \leq \mu$ also satisfies  $\lvert \xi(t,j) \rvert_{\mathcal{A}} \leq \beta(\lvert \xi(0,0) \rvert_{\mathcal{A}},t+j) + \nu$, for all $(t,j) \in \text{dom}(\xi)$. \hfill \qed

title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont{
A nonzero characteristic polynomial guarantees the quasi-Weierstrass decomposition \eqref{QWform1}, but may allow higher-index nilpotent blocks and thus physically meaningless impulsive solutions. Assumption~\ref{assump: regularity} rules these out and ensures well-defined solutions on the consistency set; see Lemma~\ref{lem: QWF}. For the power-system model in Section~\ref{sec:power}, the algebraic equations are explicit, yielding $N_q=0$, so the assumption holds automatically.}\hfill \qed

title: Assumption

For each $q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tr}}$, there exist symmetric matrices
$P_q,M_q \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ that are positive definite on
$\operatorname{span}(V_q)$ and satisfy
\[
\eta^\top
\left(
A_q^\top \Pi_q^{\mathrm{diff}\top} P_q
+
P_q \Pi_q^{\mathrm{diff}} A_q
\right)\eta
\leq
-\eta^\top M_q \eta,
\]
 
for all $\eta \in \operatorname{span}(V_q)$. \hfill \qed

label: ex: example_7_nanez
title: Example
body_md:
\@gobble{ex: example_7_nanez}
Consider the switched DAE with data $E_1=[0,1;0,0]$, $A_1 = [0, -1;1, -1]$, $b_1 = [1,0]$, $E_2=[0,0;0,1]$, $A_2=[1, 0;0, -1]$, $b_2 =[2,-2]$. The dynamics of mode $1$ are given by $\Dot{\xi}_2= -\xi_2 + 1$, $\xi_1= \xi_2$. Similarly, mode 2 has dynamics given by  $\Dot{\xi}_2= -\xi_2 - 2$ $\xi_1 = -2$. The equilibria of the two subsystems are $\xi^*_1 =[1, 1]$
 and $\xi^*_2=[-2, -2]$, respectively. 
 
                                                                                                            
               
                                                                                    
               
                                                                                                                                         
                        
                                              
                        
                     
 
The consistency sets of the two modes are $\mathcal{C}_1=\left\{[s;s]:s\in\mathbb{R}\right\}=
    \operatorname{span}
    \left\{[1;1]
    \right\}$,
        $\mathcal{C}_2=
    \left\{[-2;s]:s\in\mathbb{R}\right\}
    =[-2;0]+
    \operatorname{span}
    \left\{[0;1]\right\}$. Using the quasi-Weierstrass form, the corresponding affine
consistency projectors $\Pi_q(\xi)=L_q\xi+d_q$ are $\Pi_1(\xi)=[0,1;0,1]\xi=[\xi_2;\xi_2]$, $\Pi_2(\xi)=[0,0;0,1]\xi+[-2;0]$=$[-2;\xi_2]$. Thus, $L_1=[0,1;0,1]$, $L_2=[0,0;0,1]$, $d_1=0$, $d_2=[-2;0]$.
Similarly, the differential projectors are given by  $\Pi^{\text{diff}}_1 =[1,0;1,0]$, $\Pi^{\text{diff}}_2 =[0, 0;0,1]$. A simple computation shows that the matrices $P_1 = [1, 0; 0, 0]$ and $P_2 =[0, 0; 0, 1]$ are positive definite on $\text{span}(V_1)$ and $\text{span}(V_2)$ respectively. Choosing $O_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ and $O_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
    0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}$, yet another computation shows that the matrices $M_1 =[0,1;1,0]$ and $M_2 =[0, 0; 0, 2]$ are positive definite on
$\operatorname{span}(V_1)$ and $\operatorname{span}(V_2)$,
respectively. From these matrices, the value of $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ are $1$ and $4$, respectively. We choose $N_0 = 2$ here. 
To satify the conditions of Theorem \ref{thm:ISS_like} we take $\mu = 2$, $\theta = 0.35 \in (0, e^{\mu}/\gamma -
1)$, $\frac{1}{\tau_d} = 0.4 < \lambda/\mu = 0.5$. This implies that 
$\kappa = e^{-2}(1.35)(4) \approx 0.731$ which lies in the interval $(0,1)$ and
$\eta = \min\{\lambda - \mu\cdot \sfrac{1}{\tau_d},\, -\ln\kappa\}
= \min\{0.2,\, 0.313\} = 0.2$.
Figure \ref{fig:thm1} shows the trajectories of the system, illustrating the result of Theorem \ref{thm:ISS_like}. \hfill \qed

label: ex:spiral
title: Example
body_md:
\@gobble{ex:spiral}
To illustrate the set $\mathcal{Y}$, consider a two-mode system in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $\xi_3$ as the algebraic
variable. The dynamics of the first mode are given by $\Dot{\xi}_1= -\xi_1 - 2\xi_2$, $\Dot{\xi}_2= \phantom{-}2\xi_1 - \xi_2$, $0=\xi_3$. The second mode has dynamics $\Dot{\xi}_1= -\xi_1 + 3\xi_2 + 1$, $\Dot{\xi}_2= -3\xi_1 - \xi_2 + 3$, $0 = \xi_3 - 1$. The consistency spaces $\mathcal{C}_1=\{\xi_3=0\}$ and
$\mathcal{C}_2=\{\xi_3=1\}$ are parallel horizontal planes in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, separated by the offset in $b^q$.
In standard form, both modes share $E_1 = E_2 =[1,0,0;0,1,0;0,0,0]$ with $b_1=(0,0,0)$, $b_2=(1,3,-1)$, and $A_1=[-1,-2,0;2,-1,0;0,0,1]$, $A_2=[-1,3,0;-3,-1,0;0,0,1]$.
 
                
                                                                                                                             
              
 
The differential projectors are identical for both modes, and the
consistency projectors differ only in their affine offset: $\Pi_1^{\mathrm{diff}}=\Pi_2^{\mathrm{diff}} =[1,0,0;0,1,0;0,0,0]$, $\Pi_1(\xi)=[\xi_1,\xi_2,0]$, $\Pi_2(\xi) =[\xi_1,\xi_2,1]$, with equilibria $\xi_1^* = (0,0,0) \in \mathcal{C}_1$ and
$\xi_2^* = (1,0,1) \in \mathcal{C}_2$. The set
$\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}_1\cup\mathcal{Y}_2$
predicted by Theorem~\ref{thm: SGPAS} consists of the two
closed spiral orbits $\mathcal{Y}_1=
\overline{
\left\{
\Theta_2^t\bigl(\Pi_2(\xi_1^\star)\bigr)
:
t\geq0
\right\}}$, and $\mathcal{Y}_2=
\overline{
\left\{
\Theta_1^t\bigl(\Pi_1(\xi_2^\star)\bigr)
:
t\geq0
\right\}}$. Figure~\ref{fig:omega_limit} shows the structure of
$\mathcal{Y}$ which we recall, is the projection of the set $\mathcal{A}$ onto the $\xi$ coordinates, together with the equilibria and consistency projectors.
Figure~\ref{fig:trajectories} shows system trajectories
converging to $\mathcal{Y}$. \hfill \qed

label: rem: breakdown
title: Remark
body_md:
\@gobble{rem: breakdown}\normalfont{
This approximation requires sufficiently many concurrent requests and inference cycles per electromechanical time scale. At low arrival rates, a few requests may dominate the aggregate mode and mixing toward the stationary distribution may be slow~\cite{yang2024queueing}. Conversely, synchronized or bursty arrivals~\cite{burstgpt2024} may produce prolonged \texttt{pre} or \texttt{dec} phases, violating the independence or dwell-time assumptions. Such regimes, where the aggregate mode does not mix sufficiently fast relative to the power-system dynamics, are outside the scope of this analysis.}\qed

label: assump: flow_LMI
title: Assumption
body_md:
\@gobble{assump: flow_LMI}\normalfont{
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               
   
                   
                                                                     
                                                
                                    
                 
   
                           
                                                         
                                 
                   
                                                                                  
                                                                            
                                                                  
                  
There exist $\mu>0$, $\theta>0$ and $\kappa^\star\in(0,1)$ such that,
for each $q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{in}}$, there exists a pair of
symmetric matrices $(P_q,\tilde{N}_q)$ that are positive definite on
$\operatorname{span}(V_q)$ and satisfy the following inequalities on
$\operatorname{span}(V_q)$:
 
\begin{align}
A_q^\top \Pi_q^{\mathrm{diff},\top}P_q
+P_q\Pi_q^{\mathrm{diff}}A_q
+\frac{\mu}{\tau_d \cdot N_0} P_q
&\preceq -\tilde{N}_q,
\\
(1+\theta)
\sum_{q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{in}}}
p_{q'}\widetilde{I}_{q'}(\mu)
L_{q'}^\top P_{q'}L_{q'}
&\preceq
\kappa^\star P_q.
\end{align}}

label: thm: shds_recurrence
title: Theorem
body_md:
\@gobble{thm: shds_recurrence}
Suppose that Assumptions~\ref{assumpregdae},
\ref{assump: regularity}, and
\ref{assump: flow_LMI} hold with respect to
$\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{in}}$. Then, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
the open (relative to $C\cup D$) bounded set
\begin{equation}\@gobble{eq: recurrent_set}
    \mathcal{O}_\varepsilon \;:=\; \Bigl\{x \in C\cup D :
    |x|_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}} < r\!\left(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)\right) + \varepsilon\Bigr\},
\end{equation}
 
is uniformly globally recurrent (UGR) for the
SHDS~\eqref{eq: shds}, with $r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))=\sqrt{(c_1/c_2)\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)}$, $c_1=(1+1/\theta)$, and $c_2=e^{-\mu}\underline{p}(1-\kappa^{\star})$. \hfill $\square$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\normalfont{
Theorem~\ref{thm: shds_recurrence} establishes UGR to a neighborhood of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{in}}$ with radius $r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))$, determined by the probability-weighted residual~\eqref{eq: alpha_gamma}. Thus, from any bounded set of initial conditions, the state reaches this neighborhood with probability approaching one. If all equilibria coincide, $\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)=0$ and the Lyapunov--Foster conditions yield UGASp and recovering stochastic asymptotic stability of the set $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{in}}$.} \hfill \qed
head: environment

label: ex:stochastic
title: Example
body_md:
\@gobble{ex:stochastic}
To illustrate Theorem~\ref{thm: shds_recurrence}, we retain the
same switched DAE as in Example~\ref{ex: example_7_nanez}. The
system matrices $E_q$, $A_q$, $b_q$, and the Lyapunov matrices
$P_q$, $O_q$ are unchanged, but we replace the deterministic
switching mechanism with stochastic i.i.d.\ normalized timer-reset
values drawn from a uniform distribution. 
Specifically, for each mode transition we use
 
\begin{equation*}
    v_2 \mid v_1 = q' \;\sim\; \mathrm{Uniform}(0.1,\, N_0),
    \quad q' \in \{1,2\},
\end{equation*}
 
with $N_0 = 2$, $\mu = 6.5$, $\theta = 0.35$,
$\tau_d = 4$, and equal mode probabilities $p_1 = p_2 = 0.5$.
 
\vspace{0.1cm}
\par \noindent
The flow condition
requires $\mu\cdot \sfrac{1}{\tau_d}/N_0 < \underline{m}/\overline{p}$, i.e.\
$6.5\times 0.25/2 = 0.8125 < 1$, giving a net flow decrease rate
$\rho = 1 - 0.8125 = 0.1875 > 0$. Assumption~\ref{assump: flow_LMI} is satisfied with
 
\begin{equation*}
    \kappa = (1+\theta)\tilde{I}_q(\mu)
    = (1.35)(0.117) \approx 0.1579 < 1,
\end{equation*}
 
thereby verifying both inequalities in
Assumption~\ref{assump: flow_LMI}.
The probability-weighted residual~\eqref{eq: alpha_gamma} is $\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)
    = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\tilde{I}_q(\mu)\cdot 9
    \approx 0.5265$, where the factor $9=
\left\|
\Pi_{q'}(\xi_q^\star)-\xi_{q'}^\star
\right\|_{P_{q'}}^2$ is the same projected-equilibrium residual as in
Example~\ref{ex: example_7_nanez}, multiplied here by the
weight $\widetilde I_q(\mu)\approx0.117$, instead of the
worst-case factor $1$ appearing in $\alpha$. 
 
Figure~\ref{fig:example_stochastic} illustrates these results.
Panel~A shows the distance $|x|_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}$ remaining bounded and
repeatedly returning to a recurrent neighborhood, consistent with uniform global recurrence.
Panel~B shows the state trajectories $x_1, x_2$ oscillating under
the stochastic mode sequence.
Panel~C shows the i.i.d.\ normalized timer-reset values drawn from
$\mathrm{Uniform}[0.1,2]$. Since $\tau_d=4$, these values correspond
to nominal minimum physical dwell times in $[0.4,8]$.
\hfill \qed

    Given a set $K$, the $\Omega$-limit set from $K$, denoted by $\Omega(K)$ is defined as  $\Omega(K) \coloneqq \{z \in \mathbb{R}^n: z = \lim_{i \to \infty} \xi_i(t_i,j_i),~\xi_i \in \mathcal{S}(K), (t_i,j_i) \in \text{dom}(\xi_i),~ \lim_{i \to \infty} t_i + j_i = \infty\}$, where $\mathcal{S}(K)$ denotes the set of solutions to system \eqref{eqn:hy_sys_def} with initial conditions in $K$. \hfill \qed

label: lem: characterization
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the change of variables $(v,w) = T_q^{-1}\xi$ from
Definition~\ref{lem: QWF}. Under this change of coordinates, System \eqref{eqn: affine_DAE}
decouples as $\dot v = J_qv + b_q^d$, $N_q\dot w = w + b^a_q$. The first equation is a linear ordinary differential equation and therefore
admits a $C^1$ solution from any initial condition $v(0)\in\mathbb{R}^{n^q_1}$. For the second equation, for each fixed $q\in\mathcal{Q}$ we have that $b^a_q$ is constant, thus the
constant function $w(t)\equiv -b_q^a$ satisfies $\dot w = 0$ and
$N_q\dot w = 0 = w + b_q^q$ for every nilpotent $N_q$, so it is a
solution. We now show it is the \emph{only} admissible one: subtracting
this particular solution from any other, the difference
$\tilde w := w - (-b_q^a)$ must satisfy the homogeneous equation
$N_q\dot{\tilde w} = \tilde w$. Indeed, since $N_q$ is nilpotent, let $k \geq 1$ be smallest such that
$N_q^k = 0$. We show $N_q^i \tilde w \equiv 0$ for
$i = k-1, k-2, \ldots, 0$ by downward induction on $i$, using at each
step only the single derivative $\dot{\tilde w}$. First, we multiply $\tilde w = N_q \dot{\tilde
w}$ on the left by $N_q^{k-1}$ to get $N_q^{k-1} \tilde w = N_q^{k-1} \big(N_q \dot{\tilde w}\big)
= N_q^{k} \dot{\tilde w} = 0$, using $N_q^k = 0$. Hence $N_q^{k-1} \tilde w \equiv 0$. Now, Suppose $N_q^{i+1} \tilde w \equiv 0$ for some
$0 \leq i \leq k-2$. Since this is the identically zero function, it
is (trivially) differentiable, and $N_q^{i+1} \dot{\tilde w} = \frac{d}{dt}\big(N_q^{i+1} \tilde w\big)
\equiv 0$. Multiplying $\tilde w = N_q \dot{\tilde w}$ on the left by $N_q^i$
then gives $N_q^{i} \tilde w = N_q^{i} \big(N_q \dot{\tilde w}\big)
= N_q^{i+1} \dot{\tilde w} = 0$, so $N_q^{i} \tilde w \equiv 0$. Downward induction from $i = k-1$ to $i = 0$ yields $N_q^0 \tilde w = \tilde w
\equiv 0$, so $\tilde w \equiv 0$ is the unique $C^1$ solution of the
homogeneous equation. Hence $w(0) = -b^a_q$ is the only admissible
initial condition for the $w$-component. Therefore, a classical $C^1$ solution of $E_q\dot\xi = A_q\xi + b_q$
exists starting from $\xi_0\in\mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if the
$w$-component of $T_q^{-1}\xi_0$ equals $-b_q^a$, with the
$v$-component free. Equivalently,
 
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{C}_q
    &= \left\{\, \begin{bmatrix} V_q & W_q \end{bmatrix}
        \begin{bmatrix} v_0 \\ -b_q^a \end{bmatrix}
        \;:\; v_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{n^q_1} \,\right\} \\
    &= \left\{\, V_qv_0 - W_qb_q^a \;:\; v_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n^q_1} \,\right\}
    = \mathrm{span}(V_q) - W_qb_q^a,
\end{align*}
 
which completes the proof. \hfill $\blacksquare$

label: defn: CP

\@gobble{defn: CP}
Given a mode $q \in \mathcal{Q}$, the \emph{consistency projector} $\Pi_q : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathcal{C}_q$ of \eqref{eqn: affine_DAE} is given by $\Pi_q(\xi):=L_q \xi + d_q$, where $L_q \;:=\; T_q \begin{bmatrix} I_{n^q_1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} T^{-1}_q,$ and $d_q \;:=\; -W_q b^a_q$, and where $T_q$ and $W_q$ are given in Lemma \ref{lem: QWF}. \hfill \qed

label: lem:PD
title: Lemma
body_md:
\@gobble{lem:PD}
                                                                                                                                                                       
   Let $q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tr}}$, and let
$O_q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times \dim(\operatorname{span}(V_q))}$
have orthonormal columns satisfying \eqref{conditionspan}. Then, $P_q \succ 0$ on $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$ if and only if $O_q^\top P_q O_q \succ 0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $P_q \succ 0$ on $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$.
Let $z \in \mathbb{R}^{\dim(\operatorname{span}(V_q))}$ be nonzero.
Since $O_q$ has full column rank, $\eta := O_q z$ is nonzero, and by construction $\eta \in \operatorname{range}(O_q)
=
\operatorname{span}(V_q)$. Therefore, $z^\top O_q^\top P_q O_q z=
\eta^\top P_q \eta>0$. Since this holds for every nonzero $z$, it follows that $O_q^\top P_q O_q \succ 0$. Conversely, suppose that $O_q^\top P_q O_q \succ 0$.
Let $\eta \in \operatorname{span}(V_q)$ be nonzero.
Since the columns of $O_q$ form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{span}(V_q)$, there exists a unique nonzero vector
$z \in \mathbb{R}^{\dim(\operatorname{span}(V_q))}$ such that $\eta = O_q z$. Hence, $\eta^\top P_q \eta=z^\top O_q^\top P_q O_q z>0$. Thus, $P_q \succ 0$ on $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$.  \hfill $\blacksquare$
head: manual

label: lem: eig_vals
title: Lemma
body_md:
\@gobble{lem: eig_vals}
                                                                                     
       
                    
                                                                                                                                                                         
                                           
                   
    Let $q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{tr}}$, and let
$O_q \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times \dim(\operatorname{span}(V_q))}$
have orthonormal columns satisfying \eqref{conditionspan}. If $P_q \succ 0$ on $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$, then $\lambda_{\min}\!\left(O_q^\top P_q O_q\right)\|\eta\|^2
\leq
\eta^\top P_q \eta
\leq
\lambda_{\max}\!\left(O_q^\top P_q O_q\right)\|\eta\|^2$, for all $\eta \in \operatorname{span}(V_q)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\eta \in \operatorname{span}(V_q)$. Since the columns of
$O_q$ form an orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$,
there exists a unique vector
$z \in \mathbb{R}^{\dim(\operatorname{span}(V_q))}$ such that $\eta = O_q z$. Using $O_q^\top O_q = I$, we have $\|\eta\|^2=\|O_q z\|^2=z^\top O_q^\top O_q z=\|z\|^2$. Moreover, $\eta^\top P_q \eta=z^\top O_q^\top P_q O_q z$. Since $P_q \succ 0$ on $\operatorname{span}(V_q)$,
Lemma~3 implies that $O_q^\top P_q O_q \succ 0$. Therefore, by the standard Rayleigh quotient bounds,
\[
\lambda_{\min}\!\left(O_q^\top P_q O_q\right)\|z\|^2
\leq
z^\top O_q^\top P_q O_q z
\leq
\lambda_{\max}\!\left(O_q^\top P_q O_q\right)\|z\|^2.
\]
Using $\|z\|=\|\eta\|$ and
$\eta^\top P_q\eta=z^\top O_q^\top P_q O_q z$
gives the desired result.
\hfill $\blacksquare$

label: prop: ols_dae
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof follows similar steps as in \cite[Theorem 1]{baradaran2020omega} but uses the sharper characterization of the set $\mathcal{A}$ in Proposition \ref{prop: ols_dae}. It is clear that the set $C$ and $D$ are closed since $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{tr}}$ is finite, the interval $[0,1]$ is closed, and any finite-dimensional affine subspace is also closed. Moreover, the maps $F$ and $G$ are OSC, LB and the map $F$ is convex-valued. Therefore, system \eqref{eqn: eqiv_HI} satisfies the hybrid basic conditions. Let $K$ be chosen sufficiently large such that it contains in its interior the set $\mathcal{A}$. Following the same arguments as in \cite{baradaran2020omega}, we have that $\Omega(K)= \mathcal{A}$. From \cite[Corollary 7.7]{goebel2012hybrid}, we obtain that the set $\mathcal{A}$ is asymptotically stable for system \eqref{eqn: ideal_hybrid}. Since the preceding argument applies to every sufficiently large
compact set $K$, and such compact sets can be chosen to contain any
prescribed compact subset of the admissible state space, the basin
of attraction of $\mathcal A$ is the entire admissible state space.
Therefore, $\mathcal A$ is globally asymptotically stable for
system~\eqref{eqn: ideal_hybrid}. Now consider the inflated hybrid system $\mathcal{H}_{\epsilon}$, given by
 
\begin{align}\@gobble{eqn:inflation_1}
    x \in C_\epsilon,~~\Dot{x}\in F_\epsilon(x),~~~~~~
    x \in D_\epsilon,~~x^+\in G_\epsilon(x),  
\end{align}
 
where $\epsilon=\frac{1}{\tau_d}$, and where the data of \eqref{eqn:inflation_1} is constructed from the data of $\mathcal{H}_0$ as in \cite[Sec. 6]{teel2013lyapunov}. In particular, for $\epsilon=1/\tau_d$, the data of the system satisfy $C\subseteq C_\epsilon$, $D\subseteq D_\epsilon$, and, for every admissible state, we have $F_{\tau_d}(x)\subseteq F_\epsilon(x)$, and $G_{\tau_d}(x)\subseteq G_\epsilon(x)$. Consequently, every solution of the original system is also a solution of the inflated system
$\mathcal H_\epsilon$, and, by \cite[Thm. 7.21]{goebel2012hybrid}, the inflated hybrid system $\mathcal{H}_{\epsilon}$ renders the set $\mathcal{A}$ semi-globally practically asymptotically stable as $\epsilon\to0^+$. \hfill $\blacksquare$

label: eq: I_def
title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the function $V(x) \;=\; e^{-\mu\tau/N_0}\,\tilde\xi^\top P_q \tilde\xi$, where $\mu > 0$ is a free parameter and for each $q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}$, the matrices $P_q$ are symmetric and positive definite on
$\operatorname{span}(V_q)$.  For each $q' \in \mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}$,
define the integral
 
\begin{align}
\@gobble{eq: I_def}
    \tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu):=
    \mathbb{E}_{v_2\mid v_1=q'}\!\left[e^{-\mu v_2/N_0}\right]= \int_0^{N_0} f_{q'}(v_2)e^{-\mu v_2/N_0}dv_2,
\end{align}
where $f_{q'}$ is the probability density for $v_2$.
It can be seen that the integral $\tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu)$ is strictly positive and
monotonically decreasing in $\mu$, with $\tilde{I}_{q'}(0)=1$ and
$\tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu)\to 0$ as $\mu\to\infty$ for all three modes. For the convenience of the reader, we provide explicit expressions for $\tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu)$ in Appendix D.

Next, we show that $V$ is a
Lagrange--Foster function for the SHDS~\eqref{eq: shds} in the sense
of~\cite[Sec.~4.4.1]{teel2013lyapunov}. We begin by showing the class $\mathcal{G}_\infty$ bounds in \cite[(16a), (16b)]{teel2013lyapunov}. Indeed, note that since $\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}} \subset \mathcal{O}_\varepsilon \subset \Bar{\mathcal{O}_\varepsilon}$, we have
 
\begin{equation}
\@gobble{eqn: distance}
\lvert x\rvert_{\Bar{\mathcal{O}_\varepsilon}} \leq \lvert x \rvert_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}, \, \forall x \in C \cup D.    
\end{equation}
 
\par \noindent
Since $\tau \in [0,N_0]$, we have $e^{-\mu\tau/N_0} \in [e^{-\mu}, 1]$,
giving
\begin{equation}\@gobble{eq: shds_sandwich}
    e^{-\mu}\,\underline{p}\,|x|^2_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}
    \;\leq\; V(x) \;\leq\;
    \overline{p}\,|x|^2_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}},
    \quad \forall x \in C\cup D,
\end{equation}
where $\underline{p}$ and $\overline{p}$ are defined as in
Section~\ref{sec:formulation}, but relative to $\mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}$. Both bounding functions are class
$\mathcal{G}_\infty$. Using $\eqref{eqn: distance}$ and the lower bound in \eqref{eq: shds_sandwich}, we satisfy \cite[(16a)]{teel2013lyapunov}. The upper bound of \eqref{eq: shds_sandwich} satisfies \cite[(16b)]{teel2013lyapunov} with $\varpi(x) = \lvert x\rvert_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}$.

\smallskip \noindent
To show decrease during flows, let $x \in C$ and consider an arbitrary direction of flow $f \in F(x)$, with
worst-case $\dot\tau = -\frac{1}{\tau_d}$. We have,  $\langle \nabla V(x), f\rangle
    = e^{-\frac{\mu\tau}{N_0}}\bigl(2\tilde\xi^\top P_q\Pi_q^{\mathrm{diff}}A_q\tilde\xi\bigr)+ \frac{\mu e^{-\frac{\mu\tau}{N_0}}}{\tau_d \cdot  N_0}\tilde\xi^\top P_q\tilde\xi$. Using Assumption~\ref{assump: flow_LMI}, we get 
 
\begin{align}
    \@gobble{eq: flow_final}
    \langle \nabla V(x), f\rangle \; &\leq \;
    e^{-\mu\tau/N_0}\left(-\tilde\xi^\top \tilde{N}_q\tilde\xi \right)\leq-\lambda V(x),
\end{align}
 
where $\lambda:=\; \frac{\underline{m}}{\overline{p}} > 0$ and $\underline{m} := \min_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}}\lambda_{\min}(O_q^\top \tilde{N}_q O_q)$. Now, let $x \in D$ and $g \in G(x, v_1, v_2)$. At a jump, we have 
$\tilde\xi^+ = L_{v_1}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,v_1}$ and $\tau^+ = v_2$, and $V$ satisfies  
 
\begin{equation*}
    V(g) = e^{-\mu v_2/N_0}\,
    (L_{v_1}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,v_1})^\top P_{v_1}
    (L_{v_1}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,v_1}).
\end{equation*}
 
Using the tower property, we get
 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[V(g)\mid x]&=
\mathbb{E}_{v_1}\!\bigg[
\mathbb{E}_{v_2\mid v_1}\!\big[
e^{-\mu v_2/N_0}
\left(L_{v_1}\tilde{\xi}+\Delta_{q,v_1}\right)^\top
P_{v_1}\\
&\cdot
\left(L_{v_1}\tilde{\xi}+\Delta_{q,v_1}\right)
\big]
\bigg]
\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{v_1} \Big [ \mathbb{E}_{v_2 \lvert v_1} [e^{-\mu v_2/N_0}] \cdot  (L_{v_1}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,v_1})^\top P_{v_1} \\
     
    & \cdot (L_{v_1}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,v_1})    \Big] \\[2mm]
    &= \sum_{q'\in\mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}} p_{q'} \tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu) \cdot
       (L_{q'}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,q'})^\top P_{q'} \\
        
      & \cdot(L_{q'}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,q'}).
\end{align*}
 
Expanding and applying Young's inequality with the weight $\theta > 0$, we get $(L_{q'}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,q'})^\top P_{q'}
    (\textcolor{black}{L_{q'}}\tilde\xi + \Delta_{q,q'})
\leq (1+\theta)\,\tilde\xi^\top L_{q'}^\top P_{q'} L_{q'}\tilde\xi
    + \Bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{\theta}\Bigr)\Delta_{q,q'}^\top P_{q'}\Delta_{q,q'}$. Finally, we multiply the above inequality with $p_{q'} \tilde{I}_{q'}(\mu)$, sum over the modes $q' \in \mathcal{Q}_{\text{in}}$, and invoke the second inequality in 
Assumption~\ref{assump: flow_LMI} on the first term to get
 
\begin{equation}\@gobble{eq: jump_ineq_shds}
    \mathbb{E}[V(g)\mid x] \;\leq\;
    \kappa^*\tilde\xi^\top P_q\tilde\xi +
    \bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{\theta}\bigr)\alpha_\Gamma(\mu).
\end{equation}
 
Since $\tau = 0$ at a jump, we have $V(x)= e^0\,\tilde\xi^\top P_q\tilde\xi= \tilde\xi^\top P_q\tilde\xi$. So, $\kappa^*\tilde\xi^\top P_q\tilde\xi = \kappa^* V(x)$, giving us the final bound
 
\begin{equation}\@gobble{eq: jump_final}
    \mathbb{E}[V(g)|x]\leq \kappa^* V(x) + c, \forall x \in D,
\end{equation}
 
where $c = \bigl(1+\tfrac{1}{\theta}\bigr)\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)$.  Next, define the truncated flow and jump sets as $C^\circ := C \setminus \mathcal{O}_\varepsilon$, $D^\circ := D \setminus \mathcal{O}_\varepsilon$. For $x \in C^\circ \cup D^\circ$, we have $|x|_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}
\ge r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))+\varepsilon
> r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)),
$
and therefore $(1-\kappa^\star)V(x)-c>0$. Hence, on the truncated system, we may take $\rho(x)=
\min\left\{
\lambda V(x),
\left[(1-\kappa^\star)V(x)-c\right]_+
\right\}
>0$, where $[s]_+=\max\{0,s\}$,
to obtain the following inequalities via
$\eqref{eq: flow_final}$ and $\eqref{eq: jump_final}$: $\langle \nabla V(x), f\rangle \leq - \rho(x)$ for all $x \in C^\circ, f \in F(x)$; and $\mathbb{E}[V(g)|x] \leq V(x) - \rho(x)$ for all $x \in D^\circ.$ To show that $\rho \in \mathcal{PD}(\mathcal{O}_\varepsilon)$, define the compact set $R \coloneqq \{x \in C\cup D :
    |x|_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}} \leq r\!\left(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu)\right)\} $ and note that $(R + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \mathbb{B})\cap (C\cup D) \subset \mathcal{O}_\varepsilon$. Now, we only need to show that
$\rho(x)>0$ for all $x\in(C\cup D)\setminus R$.
Hence,
$\lvert x\rvert_{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{in}}}
>r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))$.
To that end, choose any
$x\in(C\cup D)\setminus R$ and consider the following bounds: $V(x)\ge e^{-\mu}\underline{p}|x|_{\mathcal{A}_{\text{in}}}^2 >e^{-\mu}\underline{p} r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))^2=\frac{c}{1-\kappa^{\star}} > 0$, using $r(\alpha_\Gamma(\mu))^2 = c/(e^{-\mu}\underline{p}(1-\kappa^{\star}))$. Hence, $\rho(x)>0$ for all
$x\in(C\cup D)\setminus R$, implying that
$\rho\in\mathcal{PD}(\mathcal{O}_\varepsilon)$.
 
\vspace{0.1cm}
\par \noindent
Therefore, $V$ is a Lagrange-Foster function and by Theorem \cite[4.4]{teel2013lyapunov} the set $\mathcal{O}_\varepsilon$ is uniformly globally recurrent for the SHDS \eqref{eq: shds}. \hfill $\blacksquare$
